Abstract:
Synthetic biology is a complex discipline that involves creating detailed, purpose-built designs from genetic parts. This process is often phrased as a Design-Build-Test-Learn loop, where iterative design improvements can be made, implemented, measured, and analyzed. Automation can potentially improve both the end-to-end duration of the process and the utility of data produced by the process. One of the most important considerations for the development of effective automation and quality data is a rigorous description of implicit knowledge encoded as a formal knowledge representation. The development of knowledge representation for the process poses a number of challenges, including developing effective human-machine interfaces, protecting against and repairing user error, providing flexibility for terminological mismatches, and supporting extensibility to new experimental types. We address these challenges with the DARPA SD2 Round Trip software architecture. The Round Trip is an open architecture that automates many of the key steps in the Test and Learn phases of a Design-Build-Test-Learn loop for high-throughput laboratory science. The primary contribution of the Round Trip is to assist with and otherwise automate metadata creation, curation, standardization, and linkage with experimental data. The Round Trip's focus on metadata supports fast, automated, and replicable analysis of experiments as well as experimental situational awareness and experimental interpretability. We highlight the major software components and data representations that enable the Round Trip to speed up the design and analysis of experiments by 2 orders of magnitude over prior ad hoc methods. These contributions support a number of experimental protocols and experimental types, demonstrating the Round Trip's breadth and extensibility. We describe both an illustrative use case using the Round Trip for an on-the-loop experimental campaign and overall contributions to reducing experimental analysis time and increasing data product volume in the SD2 program.

<jats:p>Materials science has hit an inflection point with AI, drawing an intense flurry of interest and enormous scales of capital across academia, tech, and traditional industry. To look forward we first take a tour through the development of modern technologies powering this new age, from shared databases to foundation machine learned interaction potentials to agentic laboratories. Drawing on lessons from pharmaceuticals, specialty chemicals design, and semiconductor design automation, we argue that the potential of AI will only be materialized with key contributions from materials scientists: richer mechanistic characterization and judicious encoding of downstream constraints.</jats:p>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Self-driving laboratories close the loop between hypothesis generation, experimental execution, and analysis, removing the human from the inner cycle of discovery. Their migration from chemistry and materials science into biomedicine introduces ethical problems that the chemistry literature does not encounter: experiments run on human-derived material, generate data about identifiable people, produce candidates intended for patients, and act on living systems whose variability can masquerade as signal. We argue that biomedical self-driving laboratories defeat the categorical triggers on which biomedical oversight depends, because what an autonomous platform will do is determined at runtime by a model rather than at review time by an investigator. We propose Proportionate Autonomy Governance, a framework that replaces protocol review with envelope review: oversight bodies approve a formally specified and machine-checkable region of experiment space together with the invariants that constrain search within it. Five duties, bounding, tracing, controlling, verifying, and answering, scale jointly with a platform’s autonomy level and consequence tier, and we specify what each requires at each position in that grid. We work the framework through a hypothetical induced pluripotent stem cell differentiation campaign, giving its envelope, autonomy annex, and accountability register, and we state what the framework costs and what it does not fix. We map current instruments onto this framework and identify where they fail to bind, and we relate the proposal to operational design domains, runtime assurance, and safety cases in established safety-critical practice. We report a search for documented safety incidents in autonomous laboratories, which returned none, and we are explicit about the limits of what that absence supports. We close with an implementation agenda.</jats:p>

                                            Abstract

                Optical microscopes are an essential tool for both the detection of disease in clinics, and
               for scientiﬁc analysis. However, in much of the world access to high-performance microscopy is
             limited by both the upfront cost and maintenance cost of the equipment. Here we present an
             open-source, 3D-printed, and fully-automated laboratory microscope, with motorised sample
             positioning and focus control.  The microscope is highly customisable, with a number of
             options readily available including trans- and epi- illumination, polarisation contrast imaging,
           and epi-ﬂorescence imaging. The OpenFlexure Microscope has been designed to enable low-
           volume manufacturing and maintenance by local personnel, vastly increasing accessibility. We
            have produced over 100 microscopes in Tanzania and Kenya for educational, scientiﬁc, and
               clinical applications, demonstrating that local manufacturing can be a viable alternative to
              international supply chains that can often be costly, slow, and unreliable.

    1  Introduction

      For centuries optical microscopy has been the foundation of scientiﬁc imaging and analysis in many
      aspects of medicine, life and physical sciences [1]. Commercially available high-end microscopes can
      provide precise motorised high-resolution imaging capabilities, however these are often prohibitively
       expensive.  This is compounded in the developing world where unreliable supply chains inﬂate
       prices, and slow acquisition [2]. Maintaining equipment adds further burden as devices have often
      not been designed for these operating environments [3], and neither manufacturers representatives
      nor spare parts are available locally, leading to much of the laboratory equipment in resource-poor
       countries being out-of-service [4].
         Open-source hardware is poised to revolutionise the distribution of scientiﬁc instrumentation,
      impacting research, local manufacturing, and education [5, 6]. Open science hardware designs are
      already in use for both research and education across a wide range of disciplines [7, 8, 9, 10, 11].

      Within research laboratories in particular, 3D printers have become an increasingly common item
       of equipment. This has led a number of open science hardware projects to use 3D printing as an
       accessible platform for locally prototyping and manufacturing laboratory-grade devices [10, 11, 12].
         Here we present the OpenFlexure Microscope (OFM), a 3D-printed, laboratory-grade auto-
     mated microscope. The OFM aims to make automated microscopy accessible both to projects with
      a modest budget in established labs, and to developing nations aiming to adopt more advanced
       scientiﬁc research technologies. It is built around a well-characterised ﬂexure mechanism [13], pro-
      viding precise 3D motion for focus and sample positioning. The range of mechanical motion is
       smaller than traditional mechanical stages, with 12 × 12 × 4 mm travel, and due to the primarily
       plastic construction, our design has a limited load capacity unsuitable for very large or heavy
      samples. However, both the range of motion, and load capacity, are ample for most microscopy
       applications. It can be constructed with a range of diﬀerent interchangeable optics modules, en-
       abling diﬀerent imaging modalities (Section 2.1) and allowing diﬀerent cameras and imaging lenses
       to be used for applications from blood smear parasitology to school teaching.
        The OFM has now been trialled in a range of applications, and reproduced by a number
       of groups around the world. The design (Figure 1) has been reﬁned to reduce assembly time,
       ease component sourcing, and maximise reliability.  These ongoing optimisations are key to a
       sustainable and useful open hardware project that is trusted for critical applications.  Version
       6.0 of the OpenFlexure Microscope represents a well tested microscopy platform, enabling the
      rapid prototyping of new instrumentation, and replication of high quality research tools, even in
      resource-poor settings.

         Outlook

          The potential impact of widespread adoption of democratized lab automation and SDLs is huge.
            User-developed automation will play an important role in providing flexible, accessible, and
             creative solutions that can make SDLs commonplace in future materials research.
            This workshop provided an opportunity to understand the state of user-developed automation
          and assess needs for the future. During the workshop, a survey of attendees was performed to
           assess community needs for democratized SDL adoption. Survey respondents (n=58) ranked
            “Developing low-cost SDL equipment and shared blueprints” as a top priority in advancing
            democratized SDLs. Over 70% of respondents shared a willingness to publish hardware
            designs and related software. The strong engagement with this workshop demonstrates that the
            accelerated experimentation community is interested in and open to wider adoption of
            democratized automation solutions. This workshop and the contributed projects provide some
             important lessons to consider as the democratized SDL movement grows.
                 Most of the contributed projects describe lowered cost compared to commercially
             available options as a motivation. The notion that user-developed automation is cheaper is
            worth critically examining. Yes, the bill of materials for the contributed projects is an order of
           magnitude or two lower than what a commercial system may have cost. However, hundreds to
           thousands of hours have been invested in these projects. While commercial tools do require
            time investment for setup and onboarding, the time and opportunity costs of pursuing in-house
            automation development are significant. The time spent on these projects is not necessarily a
             “waste”, as researchers who invest in up-skilling in SDL design and build tasks will be better
             positioned to successfully and independently troubleshoot, modify, and extend their platforms.
            Nevertheless, these costs may negate any savings on capital expenses achieved by avoiding
           commercial equipment purchases. User-developed automation can lower costs, however, when
                        it is replicated and widely adopted as an open hardware project. Initial development expenses
            are easier to accept if the project will be replicated and integrated by others in the community.
                To be widely adopted by other researchers, automation infrastructure needs
            documentation that thoroughly describes the steps required to procure, build, configure, run,
          and troubleshoot the system. Simply sharing CAD files and a list of parts to buy is not sufficient
              to empower new users to successfully leverage a project in their own work. In her closing
            keynote at the Accelerate conference, Nadya Peek described how documentation is mandatory
               for open source hardware projects. For hardware, documentation is the source—it is how a new
            user transforms a box of screws and a spool of 3D printer filament into a productive component
              of their automation ecosystem. Without documentation, there is no open hardware. However,
            supporting projects with documentation is time-intensive. Significant up-front effort is required to
            prepare complete, high-quality documentation. Supported projects also have ongoing overhead
              to keep the documentation up to date and provide direct support to new users. While these
             contributions are critical to the success of a project, they are not highly valued or incentivized by
               traditional academic currencies. New initiatives that lower barriers to developing project

              sustainability of open-source SDL infrastructure.
                  Education and knowledge sharing are important for empowering researchers to be
              effective in developing their own automation solutions. It is notable that contributors to this
           workshop did not widely describe challenges with complex, application-specific design
             challenges, but rather ‘small stuff’ like wire crimping and part design. While these are relatively
             straightforward tasks, researchers often are not formally trained in them and are left to figure
          them out on the fly when building automation tools for their work. Consider another potential
            challenge that was not widely reported: programming systems to perform desired tasks. We
            hypothesize that the lack of programming barriers is in part due to the widespread adoption of
           Python programming coursework in curriculum over the past 5-10 years. A similar coursework
            primer on electrical and mechanical design topics for students and researchers working on
          SDLs could greatly accelerate the development of automation tooling in research labs.
                                It is important to be realistic about the limits of user-developed automation and consider
             the benefits of working with commercial options. Automation involving hazardous conditions or
           components, such as high pressures or X-ray radiation, should not be built in an ad-hoc
           manner. Similarly, systems requiring fabrication or validation capabilities that are not widely
              available, such as specialized spectroscopy equipment, may be best supplied by commercial
            vendors. Opportunities exist to integrate commercial and user-developed equipment to gain the
             benefits of both. For example, the science-jubilee project integrates a commercial pipettor tool
              to provide low-cost, high-precision liquid handling, and the DiSCO project integrates an off-the-
              shelf hyperspectral imaging tool with a custom motion system to enable high-throughput
              characterization. As a community, we should engage with vendors and encourage them to
            develop products that complement user-developed automation through modular designs,
            accessible programming interfaces, and thorough documentation.
                More than anything, this workshop demonstrated the importance of solving important
           problems in SDL development as a community. We often develop our platforms in isolation and
            focus on sharing abstract updates on our system’s capabilities and exciting scientific results
            they generate. While we should ultimately be focused on the science we are enabling, there is
             also significant knowledge generated in the development of user-developed automation that is
             valuable to the community. There is no ‘one right way’ to build an SDL, as demonstrated by the
              variety of approaches to managing automation in this workshop. However, many SDL builders
            face similar challenges. Online forums are providing nascent spaces for SDL builders to share
            advice and resources.31,32 More of these opportunities are needed. This workshop provided an
             in-person exchange where builders could see platforms in action, trade advice on solving
            problems, and share their work with an interested audience. Building SDLs is hard, and building
          them in a democratized fashion with user-developed automation only adds to the challenge. The
             contributions to this workshop show that the community is rising to the challenge, and suggest
          an exciting future for democratized access to self-driving labs.

  PyLabRobot: An Open-Source, Hardware Agnostic Interface for
   Liquid-Handling Robots and Accessories


    Rick P. Wierenga1,2, Stefan Golas2, Wilson Ho2,3, Connor Coley4, Kevin M. Esvelt2,十

     1Leiden University, Leiden, the Netherlands.

   Abstract


    Liquid handling robots are often limited by proprietary programming interfaces that are only compatible
    with a single type of robot and operating system, restricting method sharing and slowing development.
    Here we present PyLabRobot, an open-source, cross-platform Python interface capable of programming
    diverse  liquid-handling  robots,  including  Hamilton  STARs,  Tecan EVOs, and  Opentron  OT-2s.
    PyLabRobot provides a universal set of commands and representations for deck layout and labware,
    enabling the control of diverse accessory devices. The interface is extensible and can work with any robot
     that manipulates liquids within a Cartesian coordinate system. We validated the system through unit tests
    and several application demonstrations, including a browser-based simulator, a position calibration tool,
    and a  path-teaching  tool  for  complex movements. PyLabRobot  provides a  flexible, open, and
     collaborative programming environment for laboratory automation.


    Keywords: Liquid handling robots, open source, standardization, laboratory automation

   Introduction

    Liquid-handling robots are versatile tools capable of automating a wide range of biology experiments. By
    replacing manual pipetting, they enable experiments to be executed in much higher throughput and with
    higher precision than is possible for humans. Robots are capable of performing many protocols, including
   mammalian tissue culture1, organoid culture2, hydrogel production3, directed evolution4, combinatorial
    drug screening5, plasmid assembly6–8, and high-throughput genomics sequencing19. Robotic platforms can
    also be integrated with computational resources such as machine learning models to perform closed-loop
    feedback control over iterated experiments9–12. However, current robots are limited by a ubiquitous
    reliance on proprietary software as the sole medium for creating and executing protocols, sharply
    constraining their flexibility, accessibility, and ability to integrate with external software resources.

     In principle, the basic operations of loading disposable tips, aspirating and dispensing precise volumes of
     liquid, moving plates, and interfacing with accessories such as plate readers are highly similar across
     liquid-handling robots, suggesting that a protocol written for one robot could be readily adapted to
    another. In practice, idiosyncratic proprietary interfaces prevent developers from creating protocols that
    are interoperable across robots. Without easy sharing and adaptation, researchers are forced to write
    programs in proprietary formats using a limited library of tools that they cannot modify or extend.
    Proprietary graphical interfaces also prevent developers from freely integrating abstractions, tools, and
     libraries which are typical in other areas of software development.

    Furthermore, because proprietary robot interfaces are typically not freely available to the public, there is
       little opportunity for newcomers to gain experience through educational, testing, or hobbyist usage. Each
    proprietary interface is an essentially unique and highly complex application that must be learned anew
     for each manufacturer, meaning proficiency does not readily translate across different robotic platforms.
    These factors sharply constrain the number of developers who can effectively program liquid-handling
    robots, resulting in an industry-wide personnel bottleneck for these roles.

   Some of the problems of proprietary interfaces are mitigated by application programming interfaces
    (APIs) such as PyHamilton13 for Hamilton robots, the C# interface for Tecan Fluents, and the HTTP API
     for Opentrons. By decoupling the programming environment from the execution environment, APIs
    provide a useful  layer  of abstraction allowing  for greater  flexibility and the use of widely known
    programming languages. However, manufacturer-specific APIs still do not allow protocols and resources
    developed  for one type  of robot  to be used on others. The issue of standardization to  facilitate
     interoperability has yet to be adequately addressed by any existing interface. Several projects to create
    standardized lab automation interfaces have been created, such as SiLA14, LabOP15, Emerald Cloud
    Lab’s Symbolic Lab Language16, and Puppeteer17, but only the last of these supports command-level
     control of liquid-handling robots, but it is not publicly available or compatible with multiple types of robots.

    Open-source  applications  outshine  proprietary  counterparts  in  their  flexibility,  accessibility, and
     compatibility with an extensive array of software development tools. Open source enables users to
    contribute changes that address their own context-specific needs and allows for integration with tools
    such as debugging and  testing  utilities18, and  AI code  assistants19.  This  allows  for  continuous
    improvement with features sourced from the widest possible pool of developers. These advantages have
    resulted in essentially all of the most widely used software development tools being open source, notably
    NumPy20, Jupyter Notebook21, PyTorch22, and countless others. Open-source software as such constitutes

13 August 2026
AI for Materials Science at Industrial Scale

Kevin Shen, Xiaopei Qin, Jonathan Scharf, Yunya Zhang, Chun Li, Qichao Hu, Kang Xu, Yumin Zhang


Abstract

Materials science has hit an inﬂection point with AI, drawing an intense ﬂurry of interest and
enormous scales of capital across academia, tech, and traditional industry. To look forward
we ﬁrst take a tour through the development of modern technologies powering this new
age, from shared databases to foundation machine learned interaction potentials to agentic
laboratories. We conceptualize the technology stack as 3 tiers (data foundations, tools, and
orchestration), trace their rapid maturation into infrastructure, and map the modern industrial
ecosystem and how prominent parties are making diﬀerent bets. We use our battery research
programme to illustrate how these AI tools can come together in an industrial setting, and
point out emerging areas stemming from challenges in materials development and translation.
Speciﬁcally, we observe that AI progress has to date concentrated on candidate generation
and low latency measurements that may or may not correlate with longer time horizon
materials development. Drawing on lessons from pharmaceuticals, specialty chemicals design,
and semiconductor design automation, we argue that the potential of AI will only be materialized
with key contributions from materials scientists: richer mechanistic characterization and
judicious encoding of downstream constraints.

1  Introduction: Why Now

Fifteen years after the Materials Genome Initiative promised to halve the time from discovery
to deployment [1], the bet is back—larger, louder, and wrapped in a different name. Machine

learning for materials is not new [2]; what changed is that search, simulation, and orchestration
became shared infrastructure rather than bespoke methods.  In one week in July 2026 the
U.S. government announced a coordinated architecture for AI-driven science: the Genesis

Mission’s federal commitments across more than fifteen agencies, DOE’s first project selections,
and the National Science Foundation’s award of twenty Programmable Cloud Laboratory
nodes—an estimated $379 million over four years, with awards starting August 1 [3, 4, 5, 6].
The lineage is explicit. The Genesis programme’s materials challenge, “Designing Materials

with Predictable Functionality,” asks for “materials design that iteratively couple[s] prediction,


                                         1synthesis, characterization, and analysis” and claims that tight integration “could significantly
reduce time to market in manufacturing—from many years to decades down to months to a
few years,” including batteries [7]. The White House’s Science: A New Golden Age report,

published the day before, puts the doctrine in one sentence: government’s job is to “shape the

arena rather than direct discovery,” because “the private sector possesses capabilities

public institutions must learn to leverage rather than replicate.” [6]

    Private capital heard the same music. Since September 2025, disclosed venture funding for

AI-for-materials companies totals, by our own tally, roughly $1.98–2.29 billion, with three firms
accounting for about 87% of it [8, 9].1 Andreessen Horowitz led Periodic Labs’ $300 million

founding round with a thesis any MRS reader can quote back: “The data in the literature is

fundamentally insufficient”—high noise in formation enthalpies, negative results unpublished,

epistemic uncertainty that “can’t be collapsed without running an experiment.” Their remedy:
“nature becomes the reinforcement learning environment.” The same memo names
industries worth “roughly $15 trillion of global GDP”—sectors AI has “barely touched

because you can’t transform them with models trained only on text.” [8] Charles Yang, writing on

Substack, put the public-private comparison in plain terms: venture investment into autonomous

labs for materials and chemistry in a single year is “comparable to the annual NSF budget

for materials, chemistry, and physics”—with the caveat, which he states himself, that VC

rounds deploy over years while agency budgets are annual. [9]
  We are not skeptical of the ambition. Energy transition, human health, semiconductor
sovereignty, defence materials—every serious roadmap for the next decade runs through a

materials bottleneck someone has to break. The historical record is full of proof that concentrated

effort pays off: lithium-ion cells from Sony’s commercial launch in 1991 to today’s gigafactories;

high-k gate dielectrics that let CMOS scale at 45 nm and beyond; carbon fibre from aerospace
curiosity to wind-turbine structural default; photoresist chemistry that tracks every node the

lithography industry prints. Those wins go beyond paper novelty. They were configurations—a

compound in a process, on a line, in a device—that survived qualification and then scaled.

   That is why the current excitement feels both justified and mis-aimed. The dominant model
behind much of this funding treats industrial materials as a discovery bottleneck: make
candidate search, generation, simulation, or instrument loops fast enough, and the path to

product compresses. We think that misreads how many materials actually get made.
   Take one of the headline stories of this new era of AI-facilitated discovery. MatterGen
(Microsoft Research, Nature 2025) is a generative model for inorganic crystals: you specify
desired properties (a target bulk modulus, say), and it proposes structures. In the flagship

experiment the team generated 32,768 candidates, narrowed to 75, attempted 4 syntheses, and

reported 1 success [10]. However, independent analysis (Juelsholt, Mater. Horiz. 2026) argued

the synthesized product was consistent with known rutile chemistry rather than a genuinely new

compound [11]. The model did what it promised: it made candidates abundant. But abundance

and retrosynthetic planning (SynAsk [80]; ASKCOS [81] and IBM RXN on the organic side). A

newer line runs the constraint in the other direction: rather than screening generated candidates
for synthesizability after the fact, Synformer generates only within the space reachable from

purchasable building blocks and reliable reaction templates [82]—a L4 generator carrying a L6

constraint, and the pattern §7 argues the whole chain needs. An example, complete academic

demonstration is USTC’s robotic AI-Chemist, which couples literature mining, computational
simulation, and fourteen task-specific workstations into a single closed loop: it screened over

three million candidate compositions and autonomously synthesized an oxygen-evolution catalyst

within six weeks [83, 84].
  On the industrial side, the planning tools working chemists actually reach for are sold
as extensions of the reaction databases they already license:  Elsevier’s Reaxys Predictive
Retrosynthesis and CAS’s SciFinder retrosynthesis planner both construct routes over their
proprietary reaction collections [85, 86], and Merck KGaA’s SYNTHIA is the commercialized
descendant of Chematica [87, 74]. Execution is a separate business. XtalPi (HKEx: 2228)
couples AI-driven design with robotic laboratory execution at commercial scale; revenue from

the segment housing that business, renamed AI4S Intelligent Solutions during 2025, grew 62.6%
year-on-year to RMB 264.7 million [88]. Chemify compiles a target molecule into executable

robotic code through a chemical programming language, then runs it on its own hardware [89, 90].

Startups such as Hours Technology (ChemPro.AI) close the loop between AI route planning and

robotic execution, while modular automation providers (Megarobo, Bioyond, X-Imaging) supply

the robotic and software building blocks from which bespoke synthesis lines are assembled.
   This family is the least mature of the five middle layers and likely the most commercially

consequential. In organic chemistry, published reaction records are abundant: databases such as

Reaxys catalog tens of millions of reactions, patent filings encode detailed synthetic routes, and

the retrosynthesis models above were trained on exactly this public record—Lowe’s extraction of

roughly 1.8 million reactions from US patents, and the USPTO-50k benchmark derived from it,
remain the substrate nearly every published retrosynthesis model is fit and scored on [91, 92].

The community has also begun to standardize what a reaction record should contain: the Open
Reaction Database defines a schema covering benchtop, high-throughput, and flow chemistry,

with a shared repository behind it [93]. In inorganic and battery-materials synthesis the record
is far thinner: atmosphere, ramp rate, precursor purity, mixing, washing, drying, electrode
processing, electrolyte formulation, and scale-up windows are rarely digitized systematically.


                                         9And in both domains the executable detail is missing: unlike crystal structures or computed
properties, process windows, scale-up parameters, and records of which routes failed and why
live in laboratory notebooks and industrial execution logs, not in public corpora. Industrial
robotic platforms running continuously generate parametric process data at a pace academic
labs cannot match. Anyone can name a target structure; differentiation at L6 tracks who can

reproduce a route at scale and log the parameters.


2.3  Tier 3: Orchestration – Agents & Autonomous Discovery (L7)

L7 routes the layers above into experiments and writes the results back to L1. The layer has

two halves, now wired together: an LLM-agent “brain” (ChemCrow, Coscientist, HoneyComb,
LLMatDesign [94, 95, 96, 97]) that couples language models to simulation codes, databases,

retrieval, and instruments, and an autonomous-laboratory “hands” (the Liverpool mobile chemist,

the Ada thin-film platform, LBNL’s A-Lab [98, 99, 100]) that carries out physical steps. Battery-
specific research agents (LLMB, AutoSEE [101, 102]) show the pattern specializing to single

domains.

    Orchestration itself became easier to build over the past year. General-purpose coding agents
matured sharply with the frontier releases of late 2025 and early 2026 [103], and individual

scientists now use them to coordinate work that once required a software team, turning ad hoc

scripts and hand-carried files into repeatable, production-grade pipelines. Software companies

are furthest along—the term of art there is the “software factory,” a standing delivery pipeline
staffed by fleets of coding agents [104, 105]. What it takes to run a materials programme the
same way, when the pipeline must end in a physical experiment rather than a merged pull

request, is the open question for this layer.
   Leeman et al.’s re-analysis of A-Lab documented product misidentification and stability

assignments that did not survive expert re-examination [106]: DFT-derived stability is not ground
truth, and human validation remains in the loop. Practitioner pushback has sharpened since
those demonstrations. Gerbrand Ceder told MIT Technology Review in late 2025 that today’s

autonomous labs still work differently from the vision, with “a lot of tool building” left to do [107];

the A-Lab authors amended their novelty framing in a January 2026 correction—materials were
new to the platform, not necessarily new to science [108]. Shared benchmarks for self-driving

laboratories remain an unmet need: a recent meta-analysis reports a median acceleration factor
of about 6× versus random sampling in experiment count—mostly on retrospective benchmarks

that tend to be easier than open-ended exploration—where programme materials still advertise
10–100× or more [109]. The credible near-term pattern pairs agents and automation with
expert oversight, using automation for routine execution while scientists validate products
and interpret ambiguous results. Integration value concentrates in coupling those tools to a

proprietary experimental feedback stream rooted at L1; individual agent frameworks and robots

are reproducible, but the loop that refreshes experimental memory after each campaign is not.


2.4 A Stack-Spanning Frontier: Multiscale Modeling

Multiscale modeling sits above the stack as a spanning frontier rather than an eighth layer:

multiscale models carry atomistic predictions through mesoscale microstructure to device-level


                                        10performance and lifetime. The capability is barely populated today (for an early attempt, see
[110]). For batteries it is decisive:  cell performance and degradation couple molecular-scale

chemistry, interfacial dynamics, and mesoscale ageing simultaneously, while data-driven lifetime
prediction still treats the cell as the unit [55]. §6 traces our battery programme’s attempt to

tighten that bridge across the layers below through concerted simulation, experimentation, and

modeling.


2.5  Conclusion

Shared databases gave every programme the same computed map. Surrogates and universal

potentials made ranking and relaxation cheap. Generative models and agentic laboratories made

proposing and iterating cheaper still. Each family expanded what we could afford to try—parallel

searches, wider chemistry, more shots on goal before anyone commits capital to a furnace or a

pilot line. None of them moved the gates that turn a candidate into a qualified configuration on

a line: scale-up, process window, abuse testing, customer sign-off. Those segments still run on

plant calendars and proprietary records, not on model releases.

   That asymmetry is now being productized. The same actors that open-sourced the middle

layers are packaging simulation, generation, and orchestration into cloud subscriptions—a shift

in who sells reversible work (computation that can be redone relatively cheaply), and at what

price. §3 maps who rents that middle and who still raises nine-figure rounds against it.


3  The Industrial Landscape

The seven-layer stack in §2 may look like a new arrival, but materials companies that ship real

products have always worked its two ends: proprietary records of formulations, processes, and

failures at one side, and a discipline for deciding what to make next at the other. When Citrine

Informatics packaged sequential-learning “guided discovery” more than a decade ago, it was less
a new idea than an old industrial instinct given a modern interface; the early self-driving-lab

company Kebotix pushed the same experiment-planning loop toward automation. What changed

over the past decade is everything in between—simulation, property prediction, generative design,

function.arguments:
{"answer": "# Open-source self-driving laboratories in chemistry and materials science

**State of the field, November 2026.** Open tools now cover much of the laboratory stack: inexpensive demonstrations of autonomous experiment selection, configurable liquid handlers and motion systems, cross-vendor control software, and automated characterization. There are credible research demonstrations and some industrial use, but few open systems have evidence of reliable, independently reproduced, end-to-end *autonomous discovery* across sites. Affordability depends on whether the price describes parts, an operational instrument, an integrated laboratory, or access to a service. (pqac-00000038, pqac-00000009, pqac-00000041)

## What counts as self-driving?

An automated instrument executes a prescribed protocol. A self-driving laboratory (SDL) also uses measurements to **choose subsequent experiments** and execute an iterative design–make–measure–learn loop. Even an instrument that adjusts dosing in response to a sensor need not choose new scientific hypotheses: the distinction matters when evaluating reported demonstrations. Lo and colleagues call inexpensive physical surrogates of more capable SDLs *frugal twins*. Their cost–capability comparison runs from dye mixing and simple titration through Jubilee and OT-2 workflows to integrated commercial synthesis and analysis; lower cost can mean narrower experiments, less precise handling, or less powerful characterization, not equivalent scientific output. (pqac-00000038, pqac-00000044, pqac-00000050, pqac-00000052)

Baird and Sparks’s *What is a minimal working example for a self-driving laboratory?* supplies the conceptual starting point; their accessible, subsequent **CLSLab:Light** build protocol makes it tangible. A Pico W controls RGB LEDs, a light sensor reports the result, and Python/Bayesian optimization selects the next settings. Required parts were listed at **$68.61 in March 2022**, excluding shipping, with setup described as under an hour. This is a genuine, small closed-loop optimization exercise—not a chemical reactor or proof that an inexpensive kit can characterize a new material. The original *Matter* article was not available in full for this review; the implementation details here come from the authors’ published protocol. (pqac-00000043, pqac-00000016)

The following comparison separates reported costs from demonstrated uses; its entries are **not like-for-like quotations**. (pqac-00000045, pqac-00000041)

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

### Where the open stack is working

* **Accessible motion and liquid handling.** Jubilee/Science-Jubilee provides an open, reconfigurable tool-changing gantry rather than a fixed-purpose chemistry instrument. The cited CdSe workflow examined **625 conditions in triplicate in less than two months**; a separate Science-Jubilee study automated silica sol–gel synthesis and connected it to small-angle X-ray scattering, reporting reproducible composition-dependent structural outcomes. These studies establish useful research workflows, but a roughly $2,000 motion platform does not include all the pipetting, sensing, X-ray access, labor, and integration necessary to reproduce them. (pqac-00000039, pqac-00000049)
* **Pragmatic hybrids.** The **commercial OT-2** offers accessible, programmable liquid handling rather than wholly open-source hardware. Its open interface makes it useful as the core of a *custom-built* SDL, provided the group adds measurement, experiment-selection software, and orchestration. An approximately **$160 Kamome** open scanner connected OT-2 preparation to optical measurements: reported timing tests were up to fourfold faster than manual positioning, and a 96-well integrated scan took less than one-third of manual time. Spectrometer and OT-2 costs are additional, and sample heating and transfer to the scanner still required human handling. (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000018, pqac-00000015)
* **Portable control software.** PyLabRobot supplies a shared Python representation of liquid-handling commands, labware and deck layouts, with demonstrations involving **Hamilton STAR, Tecan EVO and OT-2** instruments. It addresses proprietary-interface lock-in without making robot hardware free or making protocols chemically equivalent across machines. Other relevant interoperability and workflow approaches include **SiLA 2, Bluesky, ChemOS, open electronic laboratory notebooks and standards-based metadata**; instrument adapters, liquid-specific calibration, provenance and maintenance remain local work. (pqac-00000020, pqac-00000033, pqac-00000009, pqac-00000029)
* **Open measurement hardware.** OpenFlexure is a motorized, configurable, 3D-printed microscope rather than a complete SDL. Its authors reported **more than 100 built in Tanzania and Kenya**, substantially better evidence of distributed fabrication than a prototype demonstrated only by its inventors. Different optics and camera choices change both cost and performance; the accessible primary text does not justify a single universal parts price. A microscope can be integrated into an SDL, but open-source imaging alone does not close the discovery loop. (pqac-00000019, pqac-00000040)

More ambitious open hardware is emerging above the maker-kit price range. A **2026 bioRxiv preprint** describes an eight-channel, PyLabRobot-compatible liquid handler with parts costing **under $40,000**. It maintained roughly 200 cultures through measurement-driven dilution; a second build by two laboratory members took approximately **one to one-and-a-half weeks**. The authors reported lower application-specific dispensing error than manual pipetting, but this was within-team replication, the full build package was still planned for release, and the turbidostat maintained predefined setpoints rather than autonomously designing a scientific campaign. (pqac-00000046, pqac-00000034, pqac-00000051)

## Costs, adoption and reproducibility

The 2024 *Chemical Reviews* comparison puts **open hardware at roughly $100–$2,000**, general-purpose commercial hardware at **roughly $10,000**, and specialized commercial installations at **roughly $1 million**. These are *broad classes*, not matched bids with the same assay, precision, containment, service and analysis. A roughly **$7,500 starting OT-2 price** appears in the frugal-twin literature; published purchase prices vary by date and configuration. Commercial characterization may dominate the budget: NMR or HPLC–MS can cost hundreds of thousands of dollars, and neither an inexpensive gantry nor a dye-mixing demo substitutes for them. (pqac-00000045, pqac-00000005, pqac-00000044)

A particularly important omitted cost is engineering. In a 2025 workshop report, contributors described bills of materials **one to two orders of magnitude below** comparable commercial equipment, but also **hundreds to thousands of development hours**. Among **58 workshop respondents**, more than 70% said they were willing to publish hardware and software; that measures interest in sharing, **not** the fraction of laboratories using SDLs. Documentation, safety clearance, assembly, commissioning, upkeep and consumables can reverse an apparent purchase-price advantage for a one-off installation. Savings become more convincing when a well-documented design is repeatedly built and supported. (pqac-00000041, pqac-00000026)

There is stronger evidence for **particular workflows** than for widespread cross-laboratory reproducibility. At Roche, two OT-2s were integrated into its AutoLab system for FACS-control preparation and metabolite-identification work. In the reported MetID comparison, agreement with manual execution had an **intraclass correlation coefficient of 0.998**, automated replicate variation averaged **less than one-third** of manual variation, and hands-on time decreased by **30 minutes per assay**. That validates a specific industrial workflow, not autonomous experiment selection or all OT-2 assays. Jubilee’s triplicates, the silica study, Kamome’s timing and positioning tests, and OpenFlexure’s distributed manufacture likewise answer different questions: within-workflow repeatability, task performance, or buildability. The literature still lacks comparable multi-site statistics for open systems’ drift, recalibration, downtime and failure rates. (pqac-00000054, pqac-00000057, pqac-00000039, pqac-00000049, pqac-00000018, pqac-00000009)

Affordability depends on whether the price describes parts, an operational instrument, an integrated laboratory, or access to a service. (pqac-00000038, pqac-00000009, pqac-00000041)

## What counts as self-driving?

An automated instrument executes a prescribed protocol. A self-driving laboratory (SDL) also uses measurements to **choose subsequent experiments** and execute an iterative design–make–measure–learn loop. Even an instrument that adjusts dosing in response to a sensor need not choose new scientific hypotheses: the distinction matters when evaluating reported demonstrations. Lo and colleagues call inexpensive physical surrogates of more capable SDLs *frugal twins*. Their cost–capability comparison runs from dye mixing and simple titration through Jubilee and OT-2 workflows to integrated commercial synthesis and analysis; lower cost can mean narrower experiments, less precise handling, or less powerful characterization, not equivalent scientific output. (pqac-00000038, pqac-00000044, pqac-00000050, pqac-00000052)

A Pico W controls RGB LEDs, a light sensor reports the result, and Python/Bayesian optimization selects the next settings. Required parts were listed at **$68.61 in March 2022**, excluding shipping, with setup described as under an hour. This is a genuine, small closed-loop optimization exercise—not a chemical reactor or proof that an inexpensive kit can characterize a new material. The original *Matter* article was not available in full for this review; the implementation details here come from the authors’ published protocol. (pqac-00000043, pqac-00000016)

Kamome was tested with an Ocean-HDX spectrometer and Opentrons OT-2. Its scan_all() and scan_select() commands execute serpentine scans, while spectra are saved only after the system confirms that the probe has reached the target and stopped. In timing tests using a 500 ms Arduino start time and 1500 ms capture interval, Kamome reduced measurement time by up to fourfold relative to manual positioning. In the integrated 96-well workflow, OT-2 pipetting and Kamome scanning completed a full scan in less than one-third of the manual time. Reflectance tests using colored solutions correctly recovered the expected green-well positions and showed improved consistency versus manual measurements, where probe-height and positioning variation caused scattering. A perovskite thin-film demonstration measured photoluminescence from four samples with increasing chlorine-to-halide ratios and observed the expected blue shift and reduced peak intensity. These are measured demonstrations; broader claims about autonomous synthesis and machine-learning-enabled workflows are presented as future potential, not validated throughput. Positional testing found approximately 0.30 mm probe drift and 0.05–0.10 mm plate drift.

contexts.context: The excerpt supports public release of self-driving laboratory hardware and software as a means of democratizing automation. Affordable, extensible, open-source systems broaden access beyond exceptionally well-resourced institutions, allow researchers to modify and extend equipment, and can avoid vendor lock-in by using standard off-the-shelf components. Complete CAD/design files, bills of materials, procurement guidance, build/setup/operation documentation, and software interfaces are presented as important features of effective open hardware. Shared baseline platforms can support multiple workflows and scientific domains; Science-Jubilee is cited as enabling both nanomaterial synthesis and plant biology, while users modified components to improve robustness. End-user assembly also builds detailed knowledge that aids troubleshooting, maintenance, and adaptation. The principal counterarguments are substantial engineering and documentation costs, required skills in assembly and soldering, calibration/setup and troubleshooting burdens, and the absence of commercial support contracts. Proprietary systems may offer easier deployment, but integrating multiple commercial components can itself require extensive custom hardware and orchestration, with poor documentation and unavailable APIs. The excerpt also warns that undocumented user-built systems create reproducibility problems because results may only be reproducible in the originating laboratory. Mitigations include complete documentation, open licensing, standard components, modular baseline infrastructure, robust replacement parts, and community-supported projects; however, developing and supporting such projects requires effort not well rewarded in academic roles.

contexts.context: This excerpt provides a general framework for evaluating openness that can be applied to self-driving chemistry or materials laboratories, although it does not discuss laboratory hardware CAD, BOMs, firmware, orchestration code, or experimental datasets specifically. Arguments supporting public release include independent auditing, reproducibility, bias and error detection, collaborative refinement of best practices, and stronger adversarial testing. Applied to autonomous laboratories, these points support releasing designs, software, algorithms, and suitably governed data to improve transparency and allow external researchers to identify unsafe assumptions or systemic errors. The excerpt also emphasizes that openness must be selective and component-dependent. Publicly exposing operational metadata, safety mechanisms, or system internals can reveal exploitable weaknesses; attackers may reverse-engineer detection or defense systems and adapt around safeguards. Open-weight models illustrate an especially difficult governance problem because released artifacts cannot readily be recalled, controlled, or have harmful capabilities erased, and can be repurposed for dangerous or deceptive uses. Relevant mitigations indicated by the passage include structured rather than unrestricted transparency, independent external audits, adversarial testing, privacy-preserving data preparation, and careful separation of information useful for reproducibility from operational details that enable misuse. These principles map to staged access, redaction, secure testing, and controlled release for laboratory systems.

Cloud-laboratory automation may reduce access barriers and bypass practical hurdles, but development and operation can require substantial prior expertise, coding knowledge, and training. This could limit equitable adoption in academic settings and weaken hands-on learning; mitigation would include accessible interfaces, education, documentation, and support for users with minimal laboratory or programming experience. Automation does not eliminate scientific problem-solving: researchers still need to plan experiments, debug systems, and analyze data, implying that released hardware, firmware, orchestration software, and algorithms require strong documentation, calibration procedures, validation, and troubleshooting resources. Automated systems also generate comprehensive experiment and sample histories, supporting transparency and reproducibility, but centralized cloud storage introduces privacy and security risks. AWS-based access restrictions and authorized-user controls are mentioned as mitigations, while the authors caution that technical vulnerabilities and human error remain possible, requiring continual scrutiny. contexts.context: The excerpt supports publicly releasing hardware CAD, bills of materials, documentation, and related software as a way to democratize self-driving laboratories. Affordable, extensible, open systems can broaden access beyond exceptionally well-resourced groups, support local modification and repair, reduce dependence on vendor-designed functions, and enable reuse across domains. A complete BOM, procurement guidance, build/setup/operation documentation, standard off-the-shelf components, and detailed custom-part designs are presented as practical requirements. Science-Jubilee illustrates modularity: a shared XYZ-motion platform was reused for nanomaterials and plant biology, and users replaced vulnerable PLA parts with more robust SLA resin components. End-user assembly also develops knowledge useful for troubleshooting and adapting systems. However, openness transfers engineering, integration, calibration, maintenance, and support burdens to users. Assembly and troubleshooting can consume enough time to offset purchase-price savings; open systems lack commercial support contracts and require a mature project with unusually extensive documentation and support. Commercial components may be difficult to integrate because of poor documentation, absent APIs, and designs not intended for extension. The excerpt also warns that custom undocumented systems undermine reproducibility and community sharing. Mitigations include complete documentation, open licensing, reproducible component designs, robust replacement parts, shared baseline platforms, and avoiding closed, one-off systems. It does not specifically address algorithm/data release, chemical safety, biosecurity, IP, privacy, or commercial competition.

contexts.context: The OpenFlexure Microscope is an open-source, 3D-printed, fully automated microscope with motorized sample positioning and focus, Raspberry Pi/electronics options, interchangeable optics, and bright-field, polarization, and fluorescence modes. Its 12×12×4 mm travel and plastic construction limit heavy or large samples, but suit most microscopy. Designed for local manufacturing and maintenance, it addresses expensive, slow, unreliable commercial supply chains. contexts.context: The review contrasts special-purpose commercial SDL hardware (~$1M), general-purpose commercial systems (~$10K), and community open hardware ($100–2,000), though open systems require substantial software development and building. Examples include Chemputer, mobile robotic chemists, Sidekick, 3D-printed microfluidics, and pipetting tools. Open hardware lowers costs and improves customization, but technical complexity, fragmented designs, limited robustness, and weak user communities restrict adoption beyond developers. General-purpose robots are flexible but less efficient and harder to parallelize than specialized platforms; perception and decision-making remain major barriers to reliable autonomous chemistry.

contexts.context: This excerpt provides evidence relevant to open-hardware reproducibility for the purpose-built liquid handler (OLH), but it does not address Roche OT-2 adoption, OpenFlexure cost, Science Jubilee silica quantities or reproducibility, or the safety of open-source self-driving laboratories. The authors report completing a full replica build using only the bill of materials and compiled assembly guide. Two lab members completed the build over approximately 1.5 weeks, which they present as evidence that the system is reproducible and readily deployable. They qualify this claim: successful assembly requires mechanical skill, and replication exposed practical issues not evident in the initial build, including motor-cable routing that requires manual planning and finesse. These findings informed revisions to assembly, troubleshooting, and commissioning documentation. The PyLabRobot turbidostat control code was available on GitHub at the time of the excerpt. A complete open build package was planned for release after publication, including mechanical CAD, 3D-printable models, a detailed bill of materials, supplier and catalog information, wiring diagrams, I/O mappings, assembly and calibration instructions, and source code for hardware control, scheduling, and data analysis; the full package was not yet publicly posted. The excerpt concerns a feedback-controlled turbidostat and reproducible hardware/software infrastructure, not autonomous experiment design, so it should not be characterized as evidence of an autonomous SDL.

contexts.context: This excerpt concerns the OpenFlexure Microscope and does not provide the requested evidence about OT-2 adoption at Roche, Science Jubilee silica quantities or reproducibility, PyLabRobot hardware replicas, or the safety of open-source self-driving laboratories. For OpenFlexure, it reports operational and manufacturing evidence rather than a purchase price: a 10 × 10 scan with five images per position (500 images total) can be completed in under 25 minutes, or around 15 minutes at lower resolution. The software supports tile scanning, autofocus, and other plugins, and permits non-programmers to conduct experiments with control over stored data. The microscope is designed for local manufacture using open-source 3D-printable components. Assembly takes approximately 1–2 hours for an experienced builder and about twice as long for a first-time builder; individual actuators can be assembled in under five minutes. The authors also report approximately 30,000 stage-motion cycles over several months without failure when using quality components. These details support feasibility, reproducibility of fabrication, and practical performance, but the excerpt contains no OpenFlexure cost figure and no evidence relevant to the other systems or safety claims listed in the question.

contexts.context: This excerpt describes an open-source liquid-handling robot that uses commercially available motion and fluidic components, integrates eight independent pipetting channels and an on-board gripper, and has a footprint of approximately 600 mm × 600 mm. The reported parts cost is under $40,000. Its control system is Python-based, with PyLabRobot used as much as possible for software-first extensibility, protocol portability, and integration with peripherals such as plate readers, shakers, pumps, and a tip-washing module. The demonstrated application is closed-loop turbidostat-style culture maintenance across approximately 200 independent cultures, involving repeated density measurements, automated dilution, sterilization, growth-rate estimation, and setpoint maintenance. This supports evidence for a PyLabRobot-centered open hardware implementation, but the excerpt does not provide independent replication data or evidence of a separate open-hardware replica. It also does not report Roche OT-2 adoption, numbers of workflows or production uses, OpenFlexure cost, Science Jubilee silica quantities or reproducibility, or safety outcomes for open-source SDLs. Importantly, the turbidostat demonstration is automated feedback control for maintaining cultures at user-defined setpoints; the excerpt does not establish autonomous experiment design. References to self-driving labs and AI-guided design are presented as future extensions rather than demonstrated capabilities.

contexts.context: This peer-reviewed primary report documents OT-2 integration within Roche’s AutoLab workflow-orchestration environment. The excerpt explicitly describes two proof-of-concept applications: a generic pipetting workflow for FACS fluorescence-minus-one controls and deployment of one low-throughput soft-spot metabolite-identification (MetID) assay. The MetID workflow was connected to Roche databases and the Roche network, and its biological validation showed an intraclass correlation coefficient of 0.998 versus the manually executed process. Replicate coefficient of variation with the OT-2 averaged less than one-third of that obtained manually. The automation reduced hands-on time by 30 minutes per assay. However, the excerpt does not quantify overall OT-2 adoption at Roche, report a total number of workflows, or distinguish production use from proof-of-concept or validated deployment. It says only that multiple assays could theoretically run on one device. The article discusses the OT-2’s low hardware cost and potential long-term cost-effectiveness, but no OpenFlexure cost is provided. There is no information here about Science Jubilee silica quantities or reproducibility, PyLabRobot open-hardware replicas, safety of open-source scientific development platforms, or autonomous experiment design in a feedback turbidostat.
